title: Globular Cluster M4
caption: White dwarfs in the globular cluster Messier 4, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
celestial: Messier 4, NGC 6121 · constellation Scorpius · about 5500 light-years away (source figure)

recognition.text: Published in the ESA/Hubble image archive. No published rating.

story: Hubble peers deep into Messier 4, a globular cluster of several hundred thousand stars. Hidden among them, it found the oldest burned-out stars known in the Milky Way.

These are white dwarfs, the small, dying remains of stars that have used up their fuel. White dwarfs cool and fade at a steady rate, so how dim they have become works like a clock. The ancient white dwarfs in Messier 4 turn out to be about 12 to 13 billion years old.

That makes them useful for one of astronomy's biggest questions, the age of the Universe. Astronomers allowed for the time the cluster took to form after the Big Bang, and found that the white dwarfs' age agrees with earlier estimates of the Universe's age.
scale: Using the source's listed field of view (1.15 x 1.22 arcminutes) and distance (5500 light years), the frame spans roughly 1.8 × 2 light-years. Its light set out about 5,500 years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: Hubble's Wide Field and Planetary Camera 2 imaged the cluster through ultraviolet, visible and near-infrared filters. The source does not publish which color was assigned to each filter.
understand.eye: White dwarfs are extremely faint, far beyond what the eye could detect, and part of the data is ultraviolet and near-infrared light we cannot see.
